Prepare a fixed set of predictions for repeated use

Source: R/prepare_prediction.R
prepare_prediction.Rd

Compute the predictions for one fixed set of rows once and keep them in a compact snapshot. For the analytic and conditional logistic backends, the snapshot holds the prepared spatial design, so predict() on it can switch between scales and uncertainty choices without rebuilding the kernels. For joint mixed, unmarked, and other native refit models, it holds the native numerical outputs for the controls you bind. A snapshot does not add uncertainty, update the fit, or predict new locations.

Usage

prepare_prediction(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  kernel_inputs = NULL,
  max_bytes = 64 * 1024^2,
  component = NULL,
  native_args = list(),
  join_by = NULL,
  include_fixed = FALSE
)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_prediction'
predict(
  object,
  type = c("response", "link"),
  se.fit = FALSE,
  uncertainty = c("joint", "conditional"),
  interval = c("none", "confidence"),
  level = 0.95,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_prediction'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted multiScaleR object from multiScale_optim(), using backend = "profile_glm", "joint_nb2", "conditional_logit", or "joint_mixed", or the default refit backend with a supported native model in object$opt_mod. For predict(), a snapshot returned by prepare_prediction().

newdata, kernel_inputs

Prediction rows and matching spatial inputs from kernel_prep(), with the same requirements as in predict.multiScaleR(). The default NULL for both uses the rows retained from fitting.

max_bytes

Positive number. The largest allowed size of the returned snapshot, in bytes. The default, 64 * 1024^2, is 64 MiB. A larger snapshot raises an error, so use fewer rows or raise the limit. It limits the stored size, not the temporary memory used while preparing.

component

Character scalar naming the native prediction type to keep.

  • unmarked models: required. Name one component, such as "state", "det", "psi", "col", or "ext", as the fitted model supports.

  • "joint_mixed": optional. Name one native glmmTMB type, such as "zprob". The default NULL prepares both "response" and "link".

  • Other refits: the default NULL prepares "response" and "link" for lm, glm, glmmTMB, lme4, gls, and lme models, and "lp" and "risk" for Cox models. Other native providers need an explicit component.

  • Analytic and conditional logistic backends: leave NULL. Their snapshots keep every type ("response", "link", and, for conditional logistic fits, "risk").

native_args

A named list of native prediction controls to bind to the snapshot. Default list(), which keeps the native defaults. Changing any control later needs a new snapshot. Supported controls:

  • "joint_mixed": re.form, allow.new.levels, and na.action.

  • unmarked: backTransform, na.rm, appendData, level, and re.form.

  • Other refits: re.form, allow.new.levels, na.action, reference, and level (such as nlme level = 0), when the native method accepts them. Ordinary lm refits also accept interval ("confidence" for mean limits, "prediction" for future-observation limits). spaMM refits accept variances and intervals, but cross-row covariance needs point predictions instead of a snapshot. mgcv GAMs accept exclude, terms, unconditional, iterms.type, and block.size, and BAMs also accept discrete. unconditional = TRUE requests the native smoothing-parameter covariance, which adds no kernel-scale uncertainty.

Native argument abbreviations are resolved to their full names before the list is checked and are recorded by those names. Selected lme4 and spaMM effects and GAM terms are recorded in the prediction contracts.

join_by

For native refit and unmarked spatial predictions, a data frame of site keys with one row per prepared site, in kernel_inputs order. It needs both newdata and kernel_inputs. unmarked spatial snapshots require it (see prepare_unmarked_data()). The default NULL aligns general refit rows by row name, and unmarked data without spatial inputs pass unchanged. Not used by the analytic, conditional logistic, and joint mixed backends.

include_fixed

Logical. The default FALSE keeps fixed-radius predictors as explicit inputs in newdata. Set TRUE to recompute them from the spatial inputs after verifying their training preparation, as described in prepare_unmarked_data() and predict.multiScaleR(). It needs spatial inputs and verified row alignment, with explicit site keys for repeated sites and for unmarked models.

type, se.fit, uncertainty, interval, level

Output and uncertainty controls for predict() on a snapshot, with the defaults and checks of predict.multiScaleR(). For analytic and conditional logistic snapshots they choose the scale and the uncertainty summary of the fixed design. For joint mixed and refit snapshots, type selects one prepared component (the first one prepared by default), se.fit selects the cached point or standard-error output, and uncertainty must be "conditional" when standard errors or native interval attributes are returned. unmarked snapshots accept only type.

...

For predict(), any additional argument, including new prediction data, raises an error. Prepare a new snapshot for new rows. Ignored by print().

x

A multiScaleR_prediction snapshot from prepare_prediction().

Value

prepare_prediction() returns an object of class multiScaleR_prediction, printed as a one-line summary of the backend, the number of fixed predictions, and the stored size. Its elements are internal, except prediction_contract, a named list with one prediction_contract per prepared output type. Each records the quantity, its scale and conditioning, the random-effect policy, and the uncertainty restrictions. This metadata does not establish fit eligibility or interval calibration.

predict() on a snapshot returns the same output as predict.multiScaleR() would return for the original model and fixed rows. unmarked snapshots return the native table with Predicted, SE, lower, and upper columns. Joint mixed snapshots return native glmmTMB vectors or standard-error lists for the bound type and controls. Numerical outputs keep their usual structure, including native attributes.

print() returns the snapshot invisibly.

What a snapshot keeps

A snapshot binds the coefficients, covariance, selected scales, training standardization, row order, choice sets, and native controls of one call. It keeps neither raw spatial buffers nor the fitted native model, so it can be saved with saveRDS() and restored with readRDS(). Later changes to the original model or data do not update it. Call prepare_prediction() again after changing the model, locations, choice sets, metric definitions, distance units, or native controls. New data cannot be passed to predict() on a snapshot.

Supported native and analytic models keep their trained standard scaling, polynomial, and spline calls, including those inside nested expressions and formula offsets. Recovery needs one unambiguous learner's attributes per evaluated predictor. Missing or ambiguous metadata raises an error rather than learning a transformation from the prediction rows. Ordinary native lm, glm, and time-fixed unpenalized Cox snapshots use the original fitted terms for dot shortcuts and active variables, so removed variables add no prediction inputs and new data columns never enter the design.

Analytic and conditional logistic snapshots

These snapshots keep the spatial design, so predict() on them accepts the same type, se.fit, uncertainty, interval, and level choices as predict.multiScaleR(), with the same restrictions. Reuse avoids rebuilding the spatial engine when you need several summaries of the same rows. Conditional logistic snapshots without valid choice-set IDs still give linear predictors and relative scores, but they reject response probabilities and keep the reason in their response contract. Their standard errors need uncertainty = "conditional", and no scale uncertainty is added.

Native snapshots

Joint mixed, unmarked, and other refit snapshots cache the native numerical outputs for the bound controls, rather than keeping a native model or rebuilding its prediction machinery. Native warnings are recorded and repeated each time the cached output is requested. A native error in the point predictions stops preparation.

  • Joint mixed models. Point and standard-error outputs are both cached. Standard errors stay conditional on the selected scales. Zero random-effect controls use formula syntax independently of its environment, and grouping columns may be omitted when the provider permits zero-effect predictions. glmmTMB re.form = NA sets random effects to zero and does not integrate over their distribution.

  • General refits. If the provider cannot supply standard errors, the point predictions remain available and a later standard-error request repeats the recorded error. Native prediction intervals and response variances keep the provider's observation noise. Cached native intervals or variance attributes need uncertainty = "conditional", even with se.fit = FALSE. Leave the wrapper's interval = "none" when you retrieve those native outputs. GAM rows keep every formula-input requirement, including inputs to excluded terms, and the unchecked newdata.guaranteed shortcut is not supported. spaMM refits use their retained native frames to verify fixed features. An unsupported native standard-error request stays an explicit error, recorded separately from the point output.

  • unmarked models. predict() returns the cached native table. Its confidence level and back-transformation are fixed by native_args and cannot be changed at prediction time.

Unmarked snapshots

Without kernel_inputs, supply native prediction rows with spatial covariates already on their fitted scale, including raw units when the native refit used them. With kernel_inputs, supply explicit join_by keys and native prediction rows. prepare_unmarked_data() then computes the spatial columns and applies the training standardization without changing native observation or year ordering or non-spatial factor and offset inputs. Spatial snapshots keep the prediction row names and site keys in their provenance.

Ordinary occupancy and pcount state and detection terms use the original raw training transformations, fitted factor contrasts, and native component covariance. Missing contrasts can be recovered from unambiguous original main-factor columns. Other missing coding needs explicit training contrasts. Preparation verifies the fixed designs and offsets against the retained native fit. Explicit data-frame rows prepare only the requested component, while native frame inputs or an omitted newdata keep both components for native missing-row removal. ZIP outputs keep their native zero-inflation estimate and uncertainty, and every output keeps the full model's parameter count and diagnostics. Keep the original covariates and fitted designs. Frame subsets keep the original known-group columns.

gdistremoval() snapshots likewise freeze the active "lambda", "phi", "dist", or "rem" component's original training terms and native covariance, with distinct site, primary-period, and removal-interval recipes. Data-frame rows limit preparation to the requested component, and native GDR frames keep every active design and their original missing-input checks. No model or executable TMB tape is saved in the snapshot. GDR models with active formula offsets or TMB zero inflation are rejected before fitting, model selection, or prediction, as aic_tab() explains.

Conditional learned random-effect terms need precomputed training predictors. Zero-effect contexts need only their fixed design and offsets, and they reject a later conditional-effect request. Any non-NULL native re.form sets the effects to zero. It neither selects some effects nor integrates over them. For dynamic occupancy, "psi" describes initial occupancy, and "col" and "ext" describe transitions. These component predictions are distinct from smoothed or projected occupancy trajectories.

See also

predict.multiScaleR(), prediction_contract, multiScaleR-prediction, prepare_unmarked_data()

Examples

## Analytic fit from the running example: counts and two landscape layers
data("landscape_counts")
data("surv_pts")
pts <- terra::vect(surv_pts)
land <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                                package = "multiScaleR"))[[c("land1", "land2")]]
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts, land, max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                      bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
dat <- data.frame(landscape_counts, inputs$kernel_dat)
start <- glm(counts ~ site + land1 + land2, family = poisson(), data = dat)
fit <- multiScale_optim(start, inputs, backend = "profile_glm",
                        n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

## Prepare three new survey points once. Row names of new_sites match the
## prepared point IDs.
new_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts[1:3], land, max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                          bin = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
new_sites <- data.frame(site = c(-1, 0, 1))
prepared <- prepare_prediction(fit, new_sites, new_inputs)
prepared
#> Prepared multiscale predictions (profile_glm): 3 fixed predictions, 87.5 Kb.

## Several summaries of the same rows, without rebuilding the kernels
predict(prepared)                                  # expected counts
#>         1         2         3 
#> 0.6399094 1.8208897 5.2991735 
predict(prepared, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)    # log scale, joint SEs
#> $fit
#>          1          2          3 
#> -0.4464287  0.5993252  1.6675509 
#> 
#> $se.fit
#>         1         2         3 
#> 0.1998652 0.1898499 0.1614594 
#> 
#> $type
#> [1] "link"
#> 
#> $uncertainty
#> [1] "joint"
#> 
predict(prepared, interval = "confidence",
        uncertainty = "conditional")$upper         # upper 95% limits
#>         1         2         3 
#> 0.9398905 2.1443647 6.8517965 

## A native unmarked snapshot binds one component. This stored N-mixture
## fit is used in vignette("v02-user-guide").
nmix <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "cache-user-guide-nmix.rds",
                            package = "multiScaleR"))
detection <- prepare_prediction(nmix, component = "det")
head(predict(detection))   # detection probability per survey, 95% limits
#>   Predicted         SE     lower    upper
#> 1 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
#> 2 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
#> 3 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
#> 4 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
#> 5 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
#> 6 0.5106106 0.03446574 0.4432754 0.577563
